short: The five human TFAP2 proteins (TFAP2A-E, historically AP-2 alpha through epsilon) bind a pseudo-palindrome made of GCC and GGC triplets separated by exactly three bases. Each subunit contributes a basic region that inserts a loop into the major groove, and the two subunits are held together by a helix-span-helix domain; the factors are constitutive dimers even off DNA, and all paralogue combinations heterodimerize. The site is GC-rich and sits in GC-rich promoters and neural crest enhancers. TFAP2 factors behave as pioneer factors during neural crest specification, and mutations cause branchio-oculo-facial syndrome (TFAP2A) and Char syndrome (TFAP2B). A hit identifies the family, not a paralogue.
long:
## The factors

Five human genes encode this family: TFAP2A, TFAP2B, TFAP2C, TFAP2D and TFAP2E, still widely
called AP-2 alpha, beta, gamma, delta and epsilon. Each protein has an N-terminal proline- and
glutamine-rich activation domain, a basic region, and a C-terminal helix-span-helix (HSH)
dimerization domain: two amphipathic helices separated by a long span. The HSH domain drives
dimerization on its own and can be transplanted onto a foreign basic region, but it cannot bind
DNA without an adjacent basic region. AP-2 is a dimer in solution as well as on DNA, and all of
the paralogue pairs can heterodimerize; in neural crest development TFAP2A switches partners from
TFAP2C to TFAP2B as specification proceeds, and the two heterodimers open different sets of
elements. Expression is restricted rather than housekeeping: TFAP2A and TFAP2B in neural crest,
surface ectoderm, facial mesenchyme and kidney; TFAP2C in trophoblast, germ cells and luminal
breast epithelium; TFAP2D mainly in retina and midbrain; TFAP2E in olfactory epithelium. TFAP2D
is the outlier, with a divergent basic region and weaker transactivation.

## The motif

The functional element is a pseudo-palindrome of two triplets, GCC and GGC, with a three-base
spacer: GCC(N3)GGC. Older literature writes the same site as GCCYGCRGGC or in specific promoters
as GCCTGAGGC and CCCCAGGC, and databases here report both a 9-mer form (GCCTGAGGC, GCCTCAGGC) and
an extended 11-12-mer form (GCCCTBAGGGCA), which is the same core with an extra C/G pair on each
flank. The data consensus for this family, GCCTCAGGGCA, is that extended form; it does not
conflict with GCC(N3)GGC but simply includes flanking positions that are only partly informative.
The crystal structure of the TFAP2A DBD-HSH tandem domain on DNA explains the geometry: the two
flat amphipathic HSH helices stack against each other through hydrophobic contacts, and a
stabilized loop from each DBD inserts into one of two neighboring major grooves. Because the two
loops are a fixed distance apart, spacer length, not just spacer sequence, determines binding: a
three-base gap is strongly preferred and altering it costs affinity. This makes the informative
positions the GCC and GGC triplets, with the central three bases nearly free (commonly written
YAG or TCA/TGA). The five paralogues are not separable from sequence. Every model in this family's
data, across all four source databases, converges on the same GCC-N3-GGC pattern with 7-15 bits.

## Where it acts

AP-2 sites are GC-rich, so they are enriched in GC-rich and CpG-island promoters, where they can
be hard to distinguish from SP/KLF GC-boxes on loose models. The functionally important sites,
however, are largely distal: TFAP2A occupies thousands of enhancers at the neural plate border and
in specified neural crest, acting as a pioneer factor that remodels chromatin ahead of the
lineage program. In melanocytes TFAP2 paralogues bind in parallel with MITF at pigmentation genes.
In luminal breast cancer cells TFAP2C co-occupies enhancers with estrogen receptor and FOXA1 and
regulates ESR1 itself. Co-occurring motifs therefore depend on the tissue: SOX and PAX motifs in
neural crest, MITF E-boxes in melanocytes, ERE and forkhead sites in breast. AP-2 sites are common
enough in GC-rich sequence that a genome-wide scan returns very large numbers of matches; the
constraint on real occupancy is TFAP2 expression, which is narrow.

## Biology and disease

Tfap2a-null mice fail cranial neural tube closure and have severe craniofacial defects, matching
AP-2's expression in ectoderm and migrating cranial neural crest. In humans, heterozygous TFAP2A
mutations, mostly missense changes in the basic region and HSH domain, cause branchio-oculo-facial
syndrome: cervical and infra-auricular skin defects, ocular anomalies, cleft lip or palate, and
sometimes inner ear malformation and deafness. Mutations in TFAP2B cause Char syndrome, a dominant
condition combining patent ductus arteriosus, a distinctive face and hand anomalies, with a
genotype-phenotype relationship that tracks with how much DNA binding is lost. TFAP2C is amplified
and overexpressed in a subset of breast cancers, where it governs the luminal epithelial phenotype
and hormone response and higher expression predicts worse outcome on anti-hormonal therapy.
TFAP2A and TFAP2C are also required in trophoblast and germ cell programs. A structural survey of
disease mutations concluded that reduced or abolished DNA binding is the primary mechanism in
TFAP2-associated disease.

## Reading a hit

A GCC(N3)GGC match tells you that a TFAP2 dimer could bind, and nothing about which one. The five
paralogues share one matrix; assign a member from expression, and remember that the biologically
active species is often a heterodimer, so the question may have no single answer. Check the spacer
before believing a match: GCC and GGC separated by two or four bases is a much weaker site than one
separated by three, and permissive scanning tools will happily report the wrong spacing. Because
the site is GC-rich, the main false-positive risk is confusion with other GC-binding families. A
loose AP-2 model will score on SP1/KLF GC-boxes (GGGGCGGGG) and on CpG-island sequence generally;
conversely, GC-box models score on AP-2 sites. Require the discontinuous GCC...GGC arrangement
rather than a continuous GC run before calling a hit AP-2. The evidence base here is comparatively
clean: HOCOMOCO models for AP2A and AP2C are grade A with combined ChIP-seq and in vitro selection
(PSM), and the AP2B and AP2E models rest on in vitro selection alone (SM), so the family's
specificity does not depend on ChIP data. The one provenance caveat is the CIS-BP TFAP2D entry,
which is transferred from a mouse protein at 80% DNA-binding-domain identity.
caveats: All five TFAP2 paralogues share one matrix and heterodimerize freely, so a hit identifies the family only. The three-base spacer is part of the motif: check it, because loose scans report mis-spaced matches. The biggest practical risk is GC-richness. AP-2 models cross-score with SP/KLF GC-boxes and with CpG-island sequence, so a GC-rich promoter hit needs the discontinuous GCC...GGC arrangement to be credible. Genome-wide matches vastly outnumber occupied sites because TFAP2 expression is narrow. In vitro evidence supports the core specificity; the CIS-BP TFAP2D model is inferred from mouse at 80% domain identity.
